newsitem.title: USA: Latin American forces still short on rights.
newsitem.headline: Latin American forces still short on rights.

text.p: Armed forces in Latin America have still to prove they are fully committed to human rights despite a transition to peace and democracy throughout the region, the director of the Inter-American Institute of Human Rights (IIHR) said on Wednesday.
While Latin American armies professed increased respect for human rights and their records had improved, "we are not naive," Juan Mendez said. "We cannot claim victory yet."

Mendez, an Argentinian, was speaking to reporters at a conference on "Armed Forces, Democracy and Human Rights on the Threshold of the 21st Century" organised by the IHHR and the U.S. military's Panama-based Southern Command.

Defence chiefs and senior officers from 32 Latin American and Caribbean countries are attending along with academics and human rights monitors with the aim of promoting awareness and respect for human rights within military institutions.
Many armed forces in Latin America -- sometimes backed by the United States -- had appalling human rights records in an era of wars and dictatorships in the 1970s and 1980s.

But U.S. officials have lauded a new era of peace and democracy in the region, with elected governments in place in all countries except Cuba. The continent's longest war ended in December with the signing of a peace accord between the government and leftist rebels in Guatemala.
UNESCO director Federico Mayor said Latin America had moved from a period of violence to a period of tolerance.
"The armed forces must be the guarantors of democratic stability and the protection of the civilian," he said in a speech to the conference.

Mendez said it was encouraging that large delegations including senior officers were attending the event. Several militaries were instigating human rights training programmes and their records had clearly improved from the past, he said.
But he added it not was certain if this indicated a genuine desire to change or was merely a reaction to changing realities.
"We do not think a meeting like this necessarily means a change. We are not naive. We would like to see proof on the ground. We cannot claim victory yet," he said.
SouthCom commander Gen. Wesley Clark told a news briefing that instilling respect for human rights among its allies was a prime goal of the U.S. military.

Asked if it was possible for armies to defeat guerrilla movements such as those still waging war in Colombia and Peru without resorting to repressive tactics, he said: "It is not only possible, it's essential. I was in Peru and Colombia recently. One of the most important elements of counter-insurgency is gaining and maintaining the respect of the people."
He declined to comment on those countries' rights record.

Clark also said he was "not familiar" with a CIA instruction manual on torture which came to light recently. Asked if it had been used by U.S. advisors in Central America in the 1980s, he said: "So far as I know we have nothing to do with it and don't want to get involved with things like that.
